title: Anthropic IPO Said to Draw Orders Several Times the Shares on Offer
excerpt: Bloomberg reported the order book was covered on day one of the roadshow. The $70–$78 range values the Claude maker near $1.4 trillion, and bankers are said to be weighing a higher price.
body:
• Investors have placed orders for several times the shares Anthropic is selling in its initial public offering, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, a day after the roadshow began — driven by large anchor-size indications of interest.
  • The company is marketing 825 million shares at $70 to $78 under the ticker ANT, which at the top of the range would raise about $64.35 billion and value it at roughly $1.4 trillion fully diluted.
  • A concurrent $26 billion private placement to chip and cloud companies including Nvidia, Google and Microsoft takes potential proceeds to $90.4 billion.
  • Trading is targeted for November 19 on the Nasdaq; none of the order-book figures has been confirmed by Anthropic or its banks, and terms could still change.

Anthropic's initial public offering has drawn orders for several times the number of shares on offer within a day of its roadshow opening, Bloomberg News reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The people said much of the demand came from anchor-size indications of interest — large orders from prospective long-term holders — and that the order book was covered in full as soon as the offering launched. The terms could still change, and neither Anthropic nor its banks has confirmed the figures.

The deal on the table

Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, is marketing 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 each and has applied to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT. At the top of the range the base offering raises about $64.35 billion and implies a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion — up from a $965 billion valuation at its last private round, but below the roughly $2 trillion the company was said to be targeting as recently as the summer. Alongside the public offer, a private placement of about $26 billion in non-voting stock at the IPO price is being sold to a group of chip and cloud companies that, according to Bloomberg's reading of the filings, includes Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering, with 20 other banks taking part.

Why bankers may push the price

The Financial Times reported that bankers on the deal are discussing pricing above the $78 top of the marketed range, which would carry the valuation beyond $1.5 trillion, according to The Times. Morningstar puts a fair value of $1.7 trillion on the company, with a bear case of $500 billion — a spread that captures the argument around the deal. Anthropic will be the first maker of frontier AI models to go public, making its debut a live test of investor appetite for the sector after October, the worst month for the tech-heavy Nasdaq since March 2025.

The lower range was "right in line with where many in the market were valuing Anthropic before the midterms and last week's sell-off."

— Samuel Kerr, global head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, quoted by The Times

The numbers behind the demand

The filings describe growth at an unusual scale. Anthropic reported sales of $16.9 billion for the September quarter, up 46% from $11.5 billion a quarter earlier, according to its IPO paperwork. Reporting on the prospectus puts revenue for the nine months to September 30 at $33.2 billion, with run-rate revenue around $81 billion at the end of October and operating losses narrowed to $1.3 billion from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Against that sit future computing commitments of $895.4 billion, most of it data-centre contracts that must be paid regardless of usage — the figure bears will cite when the price is set.

What happens next

Pricing is expected on the evening before trading begins, with the debut targeted for November 19. Indications of interest are not binding orders, and the final price will show how much of the reported demand converts into allocations — and whether the banks use that demand to price above the range or leave something on the table for the first day's trading.
